title: Chapter 80 – The Quiet Deacon
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Mo Lian is found in the cellar, behind the old registers, on the seventeenth night of the dark.

It is Zhao Yao who finds him, and it takes six nights of looking. The cellar of the Contribution Hall is a warren of low stone rooms under the counter, lined with the ledgers of three hundred years. Each room has a lock. Each lock has a clerk. The Deacon keeps the keys on a ring at his belt, but Sun, who has been three years at the Hall and has begun to look at Zhao Yao with a tired caution, has a ring of his own.

"I do not know why you want it," Sun says, in the stairwell, in a whisper, passing over the iron key without meeting the boy's eyes. "I will not ask. I will say that I have not been into the third room in three months, and nobody else has either, and the Deacon has told me twice that it floods."

"Does it flood?"

"It is a cellar," says Sun. "Everything floods."

Jian goes down at the third watch with a shuttered lamp and a boy of fourteen at his shoulder. The stair is steep and damp. The air smells of paper rot and old ink and, beneath them, something sweet.

He knows the smell. He knew it in a trench at Green Pine Hill, on the morning after the siege. He sets his jaw and does not speak.

The third room is at the end of the passage, behind an iron door. Zhao Yao fits the key. The lock turns with a click that echoes like a gong.

Inside is a vault of gray stone shelves, ten paces deep, stacked to the ceiling with black-bound books. A drain runs along the floor. In the far corner, between the last two stacks, someone has laid a man on a straw mat, carefully, with his hands crossed on his chest and a cloth over his face.

Pebble, on his collar, goes rigid.

Still, it sends, thin and cold. Old. Empty. Nothing in.

Jian kneels. He lifts the cloth.

The face beneath is long and yellowed, with fine gray hair combed flat. It is Mo Lian's face, exactly, as he has seen it behind the scale every working day for two months. But it is not the face of a man. It is dry and thin and shrunken, like the skin of an old fruit, drawn tight over the skull. The lips are drawn back from the teeth. The eyes are closed, and the lids are sunk into their sockets as if the eyeballs beneath them had been taken out and the sockets filled with dust.

There is a black mark at the base of the throat, a fine pinprick wound, a hand's breadth below the jaw.

"He is dead," whispers Zhao Yao, from the door.

"Yes."

"How long?"

Jian holds the cloth. He is a youth of twenty-one with no panel, no scan and no training in the dead. He looks at the pale hands, the dry skin, the way the sleeve has rotted at the cuff. He looks at the straw, which is brown, with a dust of mold on its top layer. He looks at the stones around the mat, which are dry, though the drain runs.

A body drained of everything that moves. Left in a place that does not flood.

"Months," he says. "Before the Register."

Zhao Yao makes a small sound.

"He was dead before we came. Before any of us." Jian lays the cloth back. "The man who took the scale in the spring was never Mo Lian. He took the face. He took the post. He took the keys, and he put this one down here to keep." A pause. "Whoever wore him has been on this Hall's books for eight months."

Since before the Register. Since before the Garden. He turns it over, coldly. They did not come for my mother's hill. They were in the Court already, waiting for something to arrive.

"What do we do?" says Zhao Yao.

"We close the door."

"Close it?"

"We cannot report this." Jian stands. His knees ache from the stone. "If we take it to the Enforcement Hall, they will send a clerk to open the vault. The clerk will tell the Deacon. By dawn, the cellar will be clean, the mat will be gone, and the thing that wears Mo Lian will be wearing the face of a man who is very shocked." He looks at the shrunken yellow face a moment longer. "We need someone to see it happen."

"See what happen?"

"The face come off."

* * *

He spends two days on it, and does it all with his hands.

It is the strangest work of his life. He has never planned without the Interface. The panel did half his thinking; it gave the angles, the weights, the heat of a room. Now the numbers are his own. He walks the floor of the Contribution Hall at noon, as a boy walks who is looking for a lost button, and counts the flagstones. He measures the distance from the counter to the scale. He measures the scale. It is a brass beam on an iron frame, bolted to a block of black stone, and under the block there is a gap the height of a thumb where the paving has worn away.

A thumb's height.

He asks Pebble. He sits on the steps of the Hall at dusk with the pangolin on his knee, as if feeding it a crumb, and thinks the question into the bond: What is under the scale?

The reply comes slowly, as a smell comes down a long corridor. Hollow. Wide. Stone. Wall... wall. Seam. A pause. Old drain. Water went, long ago.

How wide?

Hand.

It is enough. It is the one thing in the Hall that a seamwalker knows better than any human. Under the Deacon's scale, in the gap between the block and the paving, there is a channel, narrow and dry, that runs from the counter toward the stair. A thin wedge of metal could be driven into it.

He has six pins.

He has had them in his sleeve since the Garden, six hand-lengths of grayish iron, no thicker than a straw, each tipped with a drop of resin. They were made in the forge with the aid of an Interface that is not there. They will not serve in a fight.

But a pin, fixed point-up in a seam, under a man's heel, will hold him for the length of a breath if he is not looking down.

A breath. A single breath. If I get the breath, I need a witness.

* * *

The witness is the hard part, and he finds him by accident.

Cheng Yun is sitting on the bench by the Enforcement Hall's gate when Jian comes by with a bundle of bark under his arm, as he does at noon on every sixth day. The former inspector has a book open on his knee, a thin gray volume of the Sect's regulations. He is not reading it. He is looking at the wall.

"Disciple."

"Inspector."

"I am not an inspector." The faint dry smile. "I am a man who signs his name three times a day. It is a pleasant life. I recommend it." He closes the book. "You are carrying bark. You have a Pill Hall apprentice's burden and a Pill Hall apprentice's bad color. What do you want?"

Jian sits down on the bench. He puts the bundle between them.

"A complaint," he says. "Under the Founders' Rule."

Cheng Yun turns his head.

"A Deacon of the Contribution Hall has rewritten my register," says Jian. "Eleven entries. His scale reads light by six liang in ten jin. I have a witness from the Pill Hall who weighed the same baskets. I have a copy of my own account. I do not want a war." He says it flatly, the way he said it to the Deacon. "I want a weighing, in public, under the eyes of the Hall of Enforcement, with the scale tested against a standard."

"That is a serious charge."

"It is a small one. It is about moonroot."

"It is a charge against an officer," says Cheng Yun slowly. "It would be heard by a deputy of the Hall and a clerk. It would take place in the Contribution Hall, at an hour fixed by the Deacon's own convenience." His eyes narrow. "Why do you want this?"

Jian does not look at him. He looks at the gate, at the gray stone, at the sentries in iron.

"Because I would like," he says, "the Deputy to be standing very near the scale."

The former inspector is silent for a long time.

"I do not know what you are doing," he says finally. "I want to say that clearly. I have spent a month learning not to ask." He opens the book again, and turns a page. "I will tell you that Deputy Rong is a conscientious man. He does not like surprises. He likes procedure. If you file the complaint properly, in writing, with the seal of a witness, he will come. He will come at the hour of the weighing. And he will stand," he adds, "wherever the regulations say a deputy stands."

"Where is that?"

"Two paces from the scale, on the left." Cheng Yun does not look up. "The regulations are very exact."

* * *

The weighing takes place on the twenty-first day, at the noon bell.

The Contribution Hall is full. It is always full at noon, but today the crowd is thicker and quieter than usual, because a rumor has gone through the Court since dawn: the Pill Hall boy has complained against the Deacon. The queue has broken up. Disciples stand along the walls, in the corners, on the steps outside, craning. Servants in brown pretend to sweep. The clerks sit at their long counter with their pens down.

Jian stands in front of the great scale, in his gray tunic, with a basket at his feet. Beside him is Steward Gu, unwillingly, with the small balance from the Pill Hall under his arm. On the other side stands Sun with his ink-stained cuffs. And two paces to the left, in the iron-gray of the Enforcement Hall, with a tablet in his hand and a face like a closed book, stands Deputy Rong.

He is a short square man with a gray mustache and a habit of tapping his tablet with one finger. He has looked at the scale, the basket, the complaint, and the boy, in that order. He has not yet looked at the Deacon.

The Deacon stands behind the scale with his hands folded.

He has not moved. He has not spoken. He has stood since the hour of the bell exactly as he has stood every morning for eight months: eyes lowered, shoulders level, long yellow face quite smooth. But Jian, who has spent two days learning to see with his eyes, sees now what he did not before.

The Deacon is not blinking.

He has been standing for the length of a quarter-hour. In that time, Jian has counted his own blinks, and the Deputy's, and Gu's. Mo Lian has not shut his eyes once.

He cannot.

"The complaint," says Deputy Rong, tapping the tablet, "is that the scale of the Contribution Hall reads light. The Deacon has the right to answer." He turns, at last. "Deacon?"

"The scale is old," says Mo Lian. The voice is soft and dry and unaltered. "It drifts. I have ordered it reset. The disciple's account has been corrected, and ten points added in compensation. I regret the trouble."

"You regret it."

"I do."

"Then there is no objection to a test." The Deputy lifts a finger. "A standard weight, checked against the Hall's own iron measure. If the scale is true, the complaint falls. If it is not, the Hall is entitled to an explanation." His eyes are small and gray and perfectly patient. "Clerk."

Sun carries forward a small iron cylinder, the length of a hand, stamped with a seal. He sets it in the left pan.

The beam swings. It stills.

The Deacon says, "Ten jin."

The Deputy looks. The weight, he says, is ten jin and four liang.

For a moment, nothing moves. The scale is true, then. It is perfectly true. The Deacon has had it reset. He did it two days ago, before the complaint, because he is a patient man who knows that a test is coming.

He expected it.

Jian's mouth goes dry. He had thought of this. He had counted on a light reading. Without it there is no breach, no cause, no reason for the Deputy to stay.

Move.

"Deputy," he says, in a clear small voice. "May I weigh the moonroot?"

* * *

It is a risk, and he knows it as he bends for the basket.

The moonroot is wet. It was weighed this morning at the Pill Hall, and the figures are on Gu's balance and in Gu's hand. But it has stood for three hours in the Hall, and moonroot loses moisture, and a loss of six liang would be easily explained.

It does not matter. He needs the Deacon to touch the scale.

He lifts the basket. He sets it in the left pan.

The beam dips. The Deacon, behind it, unfolds his hands.

They are long, yellow, bony. They move slowly. They come up to the beam, and the right hand closes over the weight bar, and there is a tiny, practiced motion of the thumb on the iron, a small downward pressure, as of a man testing a latch.

The beam steadies.

"Nine jin," says Mo Lian, "and four liang."

The Deputy looks. He is not the sort of man whose face changes. But he looks for a long time.

"The iron measure read ten jin four liang," he says slowly. "The same scale reads this basket at nine four. The Pill Hall steward's balance read ten and a fraction." His finger stops tapping. "Deacon, the beam moved after your hand."

"The scale is..."

"Old," says Jian. "It drifts."

The Deacon turns his head.

It is an unhurried movement, as always. The long yellow face rises. The eyes, still unblinking, come to rest on the boy in front of the scale, and for the first time since the Register they look at him without courtesy. They are flat, clear and utterly empty. They are the eyes of a creature that has done this many times before.

Jian takes a breath.

He draws Mu's blade.

* * *

It is not a drawn sword. It is a short dark knife with a notched hilt, no longer than a forearm, a key blade of the Pool grade that Lin Hu took from a dead man's belt and gave a boy who had nothing else. Jian has worn it for sixty days. He has never once drawn it in public. He draws it now, openly, in front of four hundred disciples and a deputy of the Hall of Enforcement, and sets its point to the string that binds the moonroot.

The blade sings.

It is a thin high note, like a wet finger on glass. It rises from the steel as the blade leaves its sheath, and it fills the Hall. Every head turns. A clerk drops his pen. The sound is not loud. It is only wrong, a note that does not belong in the room, and it has a direction, a clear sharp line, that runs from the knife in Jian's hand across the width of the counter and into the chest of the man behind the scale.

The Deacon flinches.

It is a tiny movement. His shoulders jerk, once, as though he had been struck between the blades. His folded hands come apart. And his face, the long yellow patient face of Mo Lian, slips.

Jian sees it with his own eyes. The skin of the cheek moves. It slides, a finger's width, across the bone beneath, and where it slid there is a line of something dark and wet and iron-colored. The mouth opens. The eyes roll upward. A thin black fluid runs down from the corner of the lip and falls on the brass of the scale with a sound like a drop of rain on tin.

"Deputy," Jian says.

Deputy Rong has already moved.

He is quicker than he looks. His hand goes to his belt, where a short iron baton hangs, and in the same instant two guards at the door step forward and the tablet drops to the floor. But the thing behind the scale does not wait. It throws itself backward, over the stone block, toward the corridor, and its legs, which are a man's legs, move with a speed no man could match.

It takes one step on the flagstone.

On the second, its heel comes down in the gap under the scale.

There is a soft metallic click.

Jian had laid the pins in the seam at dawn, one behind the other, point up, their heads covered by a drift of dust and resin. He did not know whether they would find the heel. He did not know if the thing wore shoes. He knew only that, in the Hall, in the crowded noon, at a moment when no one was looking at the floor, a Blood Shadow wearer would put his foot down on the cleanest stretch of stone it could find.

The heel comes down on four pins at once.

The thing screams.

It is not a human scream. It is a high shrill rasp, like a saw drawn across a plate, and the whole Hall hears it. It falls forward over the stone block with its right foot pinned and its left hand clawing at the brass. The false face tears. Beneath it is another: thin, gray, bald, with a mouth too wide and eyes like drops of tar. It does not look at the Deputy. It looks at Jian, and the wide mouth stretches.

"Quick," it says, in a voice that is not Mo Lian's, "little one. Quicker than I thought."

"Hold him," says the Deputy.

The guards reach it. They have iron nets, and chains, and a pair of silver pins, and they pin the thing to the floor with the skill of men who have done it before. It does not struggle. It lies on its side among the broken baskets, with the pins in its heel and the chains across its chest, and it laughs.

It is a soft, bubbling laugh. Black fluid wells from its mouth.

"You think you have caught me," it says. "How sweet."

Deputy Rong crouches. His face is white. "Who sent you?"

"Nobody sent me." The tar-black eyes close. "I was never in this room."

The body goes limp.

It does not die as a man dies. It empties. The gray skin collapses over the bones, the chest sinks, the black fluid in its mouth turns to a thin dry powder that blows away on a breath. In five heartbeats the thing on the floor is a husk, light and brittle as a wasp's nest. A scrap of something falls from its collar: a thread of black cord, knotted three times.

The Hall is utterly silent.

* * *

It is Elder Duan who breaks the silence.

He has come in by the side door with six iron-gray guards at his back, and he stands at the edge of the crowd with his heavy arms folded and his jaw like a gate. He has seen everything, Jian realizes. He did not run in. He stood at the threshold, in the shadow of the door, and watched the Deacon's face come apart.

"Clear the Hall," says Duan.

His voice is not loud. The guards move. The crowd, which has found its tongue, shrinks back toward the door in a murmur of shocked voices, and the clerks are herded behind the counter, and Sun stands with his hands over his mouth and his ink-stained cuffs trembling.

Duan crosses the floor.

He stops over the husk. He looks down at it for a long moment, his flat gray eyes traveling from the pinned heel to the chain and to the black cord. Then he turns them on Jian.

"Disciple."

"Elder."

"You have a knife."

"Yes, Elder." Jian holds it out, hilt first. His hand is very steady. "It belonged to Elder Mu of Red Ridge. He was a Pool-grade Blood Shadow, and he died in the Orchard at Green Pine Hill, in the presence of the Arbiter's deputy. The knife was given to me by Lin Hu of my clan as a spoil. It is listed in the Court's record." He swallows. "It sings in the presence of its own kind."

"It does." The Elder takes it. He turns the blade over, and the note it gives is very faint now, like a wire cooling. "I have heard of such a thing. I had not seen one." His eyes lift. "You carried a Pool-grade key into the Outer Court. You carried it under your belt for two months. You told no one."

"I told no one, Elder, because I did not know whom to tell."

"You told the Inspector."

"Inspector Cheng did not know what I meant to do."

"No. He did not." Duan's mouth thins. "He will answer for that as well." He weighs the knife in his palm. "This is evidence. It will be held by the Hall of Enforcement until the matter is closed. Do you understand?"

"Yes, Elder."

Cost.

He had known. It was the price he had chosen when he drew it: the one weapon he owned that could tell friend from enemy, taken from his belt by a man who had every right to take it. He watches the iron hand close around the hilt and feels something small and sharp turn over in his chest. He does not let it show.

"There was one man in this Hall," says Duan, "wearing the face of the Deacon. He is dead. I will have the cellar searched, the register examined, and every disciple who has had dealings with the Contribution Hall since the spring brought before the Hall." He turns to the Deputy. "Rong. Seal the building."

"Yes, Elder."

"And bring me the body."

"Elder." The Deputy has risen. His face is still white. "There is no body. It's... gone to dust."

"There is a Deacon," says Duan, "who has not been seen in eight months. If I know the Blood Shadow, there is a corpse." His eyes sweep the hall. "Find it."

Third room, thinks Jian. Behind the old registers. He says nothing. Zhao Yao, by the door, has gone the color of ash.

"The Court knows now," says Duan, to the room at large, in a voice that carries to the back wall. "A Blood Shadow thing wore an officer of the Sect for eight months. It will be rooted out. Until it is, no disciple will leave the Outer Court. No disciple will carry a blade. No disciple will speak of what he has seen here, on pain of the Hall." He turns toward the door. "Dismissed."

* * *

Jian goes out into the white noon.

The snow has begun again. It falls on the steps of the Hall and on the heads of the dispersing crowd. Ma Bao is waiting at the foot of the stair, pale and wide-eyed, with Pei clinging to his sleeve. Hua Ning is at the corner, with her arms folded, looking at him, and her expression is not dislike, for once, but something close to awe.

He walks past them. He does not answer their questions. His hands, he notices, are shaking again, and he puts them in his sleeves.

It said: I was never in this room.

He turns it over in the cold. He had thought, at the moment of the pins, that it was a boast. A last lie from a thing about to die. But the voice was wrong. The eyes were wrong. And in the last breath before it emptied, there had been a look on the gray face that he had seen once before, in the forge, on the watcher whose blood-mark had killed him mid-answer.

It was not afraid.

It was not afraid because there was nobody inside to be afraid. It was a shell. A puppet. A skin that had been taught to walk, and talk, and fold its hands, and weigh moonroot for eight months, while the thing that moved it sat somewhere else, in a cold dark room, and watched through its eyes.

The Master was never in the room.

And the Master, who has just lost a hand, has not lost his sight.

Jian stops at the foot of the stair. The snow is falling on his face. Far above, on the second landing, a figure in a gray cloak stands very still against the white, with its hood pulled forward, looking down.
